title: Do Food Bloggers Need a Website? (2026) | Jupiter
summary: Do food bloggers need a website? What social-only creators give up in ads, search and email, link-in-bio vs a recipe site, and the fastest way to launch.
body_markdown:
Do food bloggers need a website? If you're growing on Instagram or TikTok, it's easy to think the answer is no. Your audience is there, brands find you there, and posting is fast.


Our point of view: social apps are where people find you, and a website is where you get paid for it repeatedly. You can start without one, but most food creators who earn steadily end up with a recipe site of their own.


## What do you lose without a website?


Without a website, you give up three income routes that social apps can't hand you directly.


Without a site


With a recipe site


No display ad income on your recipes


Ads on every recipe page, earning per visit


Recipes can't show in Google recipe results


Recipe pages with schema can appear in search


Followers belong to the app


An email list you own and can reach any time


"Recipe in comments" posts that readers lose


A permanent page per recipe, easy to share and save


Income tied to brand budgets


Several streams that keep running between deals


The search point matters most for food. Google's


[recipe structured data guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/recipe)


explains how recipe pages earn rich results with images, ratings and cook times. A recipe in a caption has no way to show up there.


## Do food bloggers need a website to earn from ads?


Yes, display ad income needs a page to show ads on. Every reader who opens a recipe page adds ad impressions, and the earnings add up across your whole archive.


The number to watch is RPM, your earnings per 1,000 sessions or page views. It varies with niche, season and where your readers live. Our guide to


[RPM for food bloggers](https://www.jupiter.co/blog/what-is-rpm-food-bloggers-maximize-earnings)


explains how to measure and raise it.


Many ad networks have entry requirements. See


[Mediavine requirements for 2026](https://www.jupiter.co/blog/mediavine-requirements-2026-how-to-qualify)


for what one major network asks for.


## Why an email list needs a website


An email list is the one audience no app can take away. To build one, you need a place to collect sign-ups, and a recipe page is the natural spot: a reader who just saved your lasagna is the reader most likely to want next week's recipe.


Social apps decide how many followers see each post. An email goes to every subscriber's inbox, so a new recipe can reach your most loyal readers the day it goes live. That steady return traffic also lifts ad income on the site.


## Link-in-bio vs a real recipe site


A link-in-bio page is a menu. A recipe site is the meal.


Link-in-bio tools are good for listing a few destinations from your profile. They don't hold the full recipe, they don't carry ads on that recipe, and they don't give each dish its own page that can rank in Google.


A recipe site does all of that on one page: the method, the photos, the ads, and a shoppable ingredient list readers can send to a grocery cart. The two can work together, with the bio link pointing straight to recipe pages.

## What is the fastest way to get a site live?


The fastest way is a hosted platform built for recipes. Building a theme yourself means choosing hosting, a recipe card plugin, schema settings, ad setup and image sizes before you publish anything.


If you want to compare options, our guide to


[the best free platforms to start a recipe blog](https://www.jupiter.co/blog/best-free-platforms-start-recipe-blog-2026)


covers the trade-offs. For the full setup from scratch, see


[how to start a food blog and make money](https://www.jupiter.co/blog/how-to-start-a-food-blog-and-make-money-2026)


.


Whichever route you pick, start with the recipes your followers already ask for. Those pages have built-in demand from day one.


## When is Instagram-only fine?


Staying social-only is a fair choice in a few cases:


-


Most of your income is brand deals, and you're happy for it to stay that way.


-


You post food content that isn't recipes, such as restaurant reviews or travel.


-


You're testing whether you enjoy creating before you commit more time.


Even then, keep a backup. An email list, even a small one, means a reach change or a lost account doesn't erase your audience. Google's guidance on


[creating helpful content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content)


is also worth reading before you write your first recipe pages.


## How a website fits your growth plan


A website works best as part of a system: social posts bring new people in, recipe pages earn from them, and email brings them back. The

shows how the pieces connect.
